overview: Miners barely react to the AI Plateau, though some point out that driverless haul trucks already work without any clever AI. Under Steady Disruption most expect a scramble for fewer seats in a surface control room, so they sign up for training and lean on the union, while AGI by 2028 alarms most of them: worry jumps to 3.6 out of 5 and they cut spending and turn to family, church, the union and the state. AGI by 2031 brings hard saving and retraining, AGI by 2036 feels mostly manageable, and in every scenario miners who adapt easily and have savings stay calmest while those who resist change or have little put away worry most.

S0.headline: Almost every miner carries on as before, calm and a little relieved, though a few still see driverless trucks coming either way.

whatTheyDo.text: Nearly all keep doing their shifts and change nothing big, such as staying on the loader until the kids finish school or counting down to a planned retirement.
Just under half keep building savings, for example putting a set amount each fortnight towards a house deposit, a wedding or a bigger buffer.

A similar share keep using AI tools for small jobs, such as writing shift and safety reports, checking pay slips or studying for the next ticket. This is almost all adaptable miners; those who resist change don't touch it.
About one in seven keep growing a weekend business, such as hiring out mini-excavators or doing drone surveys for farmers.
About one in seven stay active in the union, often pushing for a clause that stops driverless trucks coming in without talks first.

S0.whatTheySay: Most say "I told you so": city people and head office get excited about every gadget, and someone still has to push the dirt. They say it at break time, after church or at the union meeting rather than online.
S0.whatTheyThink: Privately most are relieved that their plans hold, whether that's a wedding, a mortgage or finishing their last few years in the cab. A few say the real threat was never chatbots but driverless trucks, which already run on GPS and sensors, so their job could still go slowly.
S0.howTheyFeel: Calm, often thankful or a little smug. A small number feel a nagging worry every time they pass the empty cabs in the next pit.

differences.text: Almost all adaptive miners (94%) keep learning AI tools and a third invest or run a side business, while none of the resistant ones use AI at all.
Miners on the lowest rungs save more (60%) than senior ones (32%).
Progressive miners are the only ones who stay busy in the union (40%), and they hold most of the little unease there is, with average worry at 1.12 against 1.00 for others.

quotes.name: Vera Zhang
quotes.text: They didn't need AI to get rid of the drivers up north. They just needed GPS and a bean counter.

quotes.name: Vera Patel
quotes.text: The technology people overpromise, the doom people overreact, and the truth is usually boring.

quotes.name: Hassan Fischer
quotes.text: If AI stays a tool, I'll just be the old man who's weirdly good with it.

S1.headline: Most miners expect their machines to be run from a surface control room with fewer people, so they line up for training and ask the union to make the change fair.

whatTheyDo.text: About half sign up for remote-control training, where you run the loader, drill or truck from a room on the surface. Many wait until two or three crewmates have done it and say it works.
Almost as many use AI apps more, often to understand manuals or practise for written tests.
About four in ten hold on to money, such as putting the kitchen renovation or a new car budget into savings.
A third push the union for a written deal: paid training on work time, current workers first in line for the new seats and no forced redundancies.
About three in ten cut back, dropping takeaway nights, a streaming service or a second phone plan.

S1.whatTheySay: Most say change is fine if it's fair and workers get a say. Progressive miners want the union at the table from day one, while traditional ones say the company has a right to bring in machines but should train its own people first.
S1.whatTheyThink: Privately many think one person will watch three machines, so most of the crew won't be needed, and they wonder whether they'll be picked. Some like the idea of working in air conditioning out of the dust.
S1.howTheyFeel: Mostly uneasy, often likened to listening for the roof working underground. Some are calm or even excited, and about a fifth are anxious.

differences.text: Worry falls from 2.6 among resistant miners to 1.1 among adaptive ones. Adaptive miners train (72%) and learn AI (91%), while resistant ones cut spending (62%) and wait to see what the company does (56%).
Worry rises from 1.6 for miners with strong savings to 2.3 for those with thin savings, and cutting spending jumps from 5% to 56%.
Every progressive miner turns to the union, while centre and traditional miners don't; instead about four in ten of them wait and see.

quotes.name: Aisha Yilmaz
quotes.text: Part of me likes the idea of a job with air conditioning. Part of me is counting the chairs in that control room.

quotes.name: Diego Farah
quotes.text: The ones who'll get picked aren't the best miners. They're the ones who are good on a computer, and that's not the same thing.

quotes.name: Olga Chen
quotes.text: I'd rather fight for the jobs we've got than pretend I'm going to become a computer person at 43.

S2.headline: Most miners are alarmed by AGI arriving in two years, and they cut spending hard and look to family, church, the union or the state to keep the house.

whatTheyDo.text: Nearly two thirds cut back at once, going through every bill, selling a boat or car and dropping trips, football fees and streaming.
More than half plan to lean on others, such as moving in with parents or a brother, going to the pastor, asking the bank for a mortgage break or applying for government support.
Over a third get political, writing to their member of parliament or campaigning for a basic income, meaning a regular payment to everyone, or a tax on companies that use robots.
About a third hold on to cash, for example freezing a house purchase and keeping the deposit as safety money.
Just under a third push the union to protest, or to demand at least a year's wages in redundancy pay.

S2.whatTheySay: Most say it's far too fast and that someone should have put on the brakes. Many want the government to step in, and even those who'd rather families pull together admit they'd take the help.
S2.whatTheyThink: Privately most think even the remote-control seat goes if AI can drive and fix the machine itself. Many fear losing both household incomes at once, and some fear the whole mining town emptying out.
S2.howTheyFeel: Alarmed or anxious, with many lying awake doing sums. About one in ten feel panicked, as if the ground has gone.

differences.text: Worry rises from 3.0 among adaptive miners to 4.2 among resistant ones. Resistant miners mostly seek support (81%) and cut spending (79%), while adaptive ones look for new jobs (43%) or side income (35%).
Worry rises from 3.2 for miners with strong savings to 4.0 for those with thin savings, who seek support far more (78% against 43%).
Progressive miners turn to the union (85%) and politics (83%), while traditional miners lean on family and church (78% seek support) and make family plans (37%).
Nearly four in ten miners late in their careers plan to retire early, and their worry (3.5) is a little lower than mid-career miners (3.8).

quotes.name: Chloe Dubois
quotes.text: Kellerton exists because of Red Hill, so if Red Hill doesn't need people, Kellerton is just houses.

quotes.name: Maya Wagner
quotes.text: We've always had one leg to stand on. This would be the first time both legs go at once.

quotes.name: Kira Silva
quotes.text: I'm not scared for me, but it's a heavy thing to be the one who's fine.

S3.headline: Most miners see five years as a short but usable window, so they save hard and start a second skill while the mine still pays.

whatTheyDo.text: More than three quarters save hard, such as banking overtime, paying extra off the mortgage or building savings from a few months towards a year.
More than half train for something next, often the remote-control course first and then a part-time electrical, maintenance or safety qualification.
About three in ten build a side business, such as fencing, earthworks with a second-hand mini-excavator or drone surveys.
About a quarter push the union to get a signed deal on retraining and redundancy before the robots arrive.
Just under a quarter invest, for example buying machines they can own or putting money into robot companies.

S3.whatTheySay: Most say five years is enough if people start now, and that the company and government should fund training. Traditional miners add that it should be apprenticeships and real jobs, not handouts.
S3.whatTheyThink: Privately many think the ending is the same, just slower: a few more years on the machine or in the control room, then out. Older miners work out whether they can reach retirement first.
S3.howTheyFeel: Anxious or uneasy, but able to breathe, like a long ramp instead of a cliff. A smaller group still feel alarmed.

differences.text: Worry falls from 3.4 among resistant miners to 1.9 among adaptive ones. Resistant miners mostly save (96%) and keep going (40%), while adaptive ones retrain (69%) and build side income (52%).

Worry rises from 2.2 for miners with strong savings to 3.0 for those with thin savings. Almost all with thin savings save harder (93%), while those with strong savings invest far more (44% against 7%).
Late-career miners worry less (2.4 against 2.8 mid-career), and more of them simply keep going (33%) or plan to retire early (21%).
Most progressive miners join union efforts (73%), while centre and traditional miners don't.

quotes.name: Olga Novak
quotes.text: Five years would get me to being a good truck driver, right at the moment nobody needs one.

quotes.name: Umar Weber
quotes.text: In five years I can own the robots. In two years I'm just racing them.

quotes.name: Maya Larsen
quotes.text: Two years is a door slamming. Five years is a door closing slowly, and you can get your coat and say goodbye to people on the way out.

S4.headline: With ten years' warning, most miners carry on working and plan calmly around family, retirement and a gradual move into new work.

whatTheyDo.text: More than half keep working much as before, especially those who'll retire before the robots arrive.
About half plan around family, such as timing a baby or a wedding, or steering their children towards trades that will last instead of the mine.
About half save steadily and aim to own their house outright before the change lands.
About four in ten start a course at an easy pace, often once they see the first automated machines on their own site.
Nearly three in ten invest, for example buying automated diggers for a family business or putting money into broad funds that include robot companies.

S4.whatTheySay: Most say ten years is plenty, so nobody has an excuse to be caught out. Progressive miners aim that at the government and companies, while traditional ones say people should take responsibility themselves.
S4.whatTheyThink: Privately many think it works out for them, with the mortgage smaller and the kids grown by then, and older miners expect to be retired. The worry that's left is often for younger workers, their own children and the town.
S4.howTheyFeel: Mostly uneasy or calm, like a low hum rather than a siren. About one in eight still feel anxious or alarmed.

differences.text: Worry falls from 2.3 among resistant miners to 1.2 among adaptive ones. Most resistant miners just keep going (89%), while adaptive ones invest (59%) and build side income (56%).
Late-career miners are calmest (1.5 against 2.0 mid-career), and most keep going until retirement (89%), while early and mid-career miners retrain (57%).
Worry falls from 2.0 for miners with thin savings to 1.5 for those with strong savings.
Progressive miners stay active in the union (69%), while traditional miners focus on family plans (67%).

quotes.name: Vera Zhang
quotes.text: Ten years is a gift, and this town has a habit of leaving gifts in the wrapping.

quotes.name: Liam Schmidt
quotes.text: You still enjoy it, but you're always counting.

quotes.name: Rosa Diaz
quotes.text: Ten years turns a survival plan into a proper business plan.
